title: Dedupe, keep order
prompt: Remove duplicates from arr, keeping first-seen order.
explanation: A Set drops duplicates and keeps insertion order. Spread it back into an array.
hint: Which built-in collection rejects duplicates and remembers insertion order?

title: Numeric sort, no mutation
prompt: Get a sorted copy of nums, ascending, without changing nums.

traps.why: Sorts correctly, but sort works in place, so nums changes too.
No comparator means string order: [10, 9] stays [10, 9].

explanation: Copy first, then sort with a numeric comparator. ES2023's toSorted does both.
hint: Copy first, then sort with a comparator. ES2023 also has a non-mutating sort.

title: m × n grid of zeros
prompt: Create an m × n grid filled with 0.
accept: Array.from({ length: m }, () => Array.from({ length: n }, () => 0))

traps.why: fill puts the same row object in every slot. grid[0][0] = 1 changes every row.
Array(m) is all holes, and map skips holes, so you get an empty sparse array.

explanation: Each row has to be a separate array, so build rows with a factory function.
hint: Every row has to be a different array. What does fill put in each slot?

title: Frequency map
prompt: Count how often each value in arr appears, as a Map.
explanation: Map.set returns the map, so it chains nicely inside reduce. A for...of loop is just as good in an interview.
hint: reduce into a new Map(). What does map.set return?

title: Sum an array
prompt: Sum the numbers in nums. It must also work when nums is empty.

traps.why: Without the initial 0, an empty array throws a TypeError.

explanation: Always pass the initial value. It also fixes the type of the accumulator.
hint: What does reduce do with an empty array and no starting value?

title: Last element

traps.why: That reads a property named "-1", which is undefined. Negative indexes only work with .at().

explanation: at() accepts negative indexes. Handy for stacks: stack.at(-1) is peek.
hint: There's an array method that accepts negative indexes.

title: Range 0..n-1

traps.why: Array(n) has holes, and map skips holes, so nothing is filled in.

explanation: Array.from passes (value, index) to its mapper, even for slots that don't exist yet.
hint: Array.from takes a length and a mapper that receives the index.

title: Max of an array

traps.why: Math.max takes separate arguments. Given an array, it converts it to a number and returns NaN.

explanation: Spread the array into arguments. For very large arrays (100k+ items), use reduce instead to avoid argument limits.
hint: Math.max wants separate arguments, not one array.

title: Reverse a string

traps.why: Strings are immutable and have no reverse method. Go through an array.

explanation: String → array → reverse → join. [...s] also keeps emoji intact, which split('') doesn't.
hint: Strings can't be reversed directly. Which type can?

title: Swap two elements
prompt: Swap a[i] and a[j] without a temp variable.
explanation: Destructuring assignment builds the right-hand array first, then assigns. If the previous line has no semicolon, a line starting with [ can join onto it.
hint: Destructuring works on the left side of = too.

title: Letter to index
prompt: Turn a lowercase letter ch into 0–25 (a → 0, z → 25).

traps.why: That works in C or Java, but in JS subtracting strings converts them to numbers: NaN.

explanation: Character codes for a–z are 97–122. Useful for 26-slot count arrays in anagram problems.

title: Deep copy
prompt: Make a deep copy of obj (nested objects, Dates and Maps included).

traps.why: Spread is shallow: nested objects are still shared.
Works for plain data, but Dates become strings, Maps become {}, and undefined values disappear.

explanation: structuredClone is built into browsers and Node 17+, and handles Dates, Maps, Sets and cycles.
hint: There's a built-in global function for exactly this.
